Issued at 134 PM CDT Tue Sep 15 2026

Per regional surface analyses charts, a stout 996mb surface low
is currently moving through central Ontario. A cold front 
extends south of the low through central Wisconsin through 
eastern Iowa. Meanwhile, showers and thunderstorms continue to 
fester within a low- level warm air advection regime ahead of 
the cold front from the central Plains through northern Illinois
and central Lower Michigan. Broad low-level confluence across 
the Lower Great Lakes ahead of the front is leading to pooling 
of low-level moisture as confirmed by surface dew points rising 
into the upper 60s to lower 70s early this afternoon. A stout 
temperature gradient is also present across the area (thanks to 
morning clouds with northern extent), with current temperatures 
ranging from the lower 70s near the Wisconsin state line to 
lower 90s near the US-24 corridor. It definitely feels more warm
and humid out there today compared to yesterday. 

Current expectations are that the continued warming of the 
moistening boundary layer will support the redevelopment of 
showers and thunderstorms by mid afternoon. Initial activity may
originate out of a remnant mid-level boundary currently 
stretching just northwest of the I-55 corridor before expanding 
near and south of I-80 by sunset as the aforementioned cold 
front arrives and stalls across the area. Some 35 to 40 kt of 
upper-level flow atop the instability axis (on the southern side
of an upper-level jet focused in the Upper Great Lakes) will 
provide some means for localized clustering or even brief 
supercellular structures this afternoon and evening supporting a
low-end (level 1 out of 5) threat for localized damaging winds 
or even a funnel cloud. 

After dark, a somewhat broad and unfocused but nevertheless 
persistent low-level jet will develop and override the stalled 
frontal boundary across the middle Mississippi River Valley. At 
the same time, a broad region of mid-level warm air advection 
across the central US ahead of a diving Pacific trough will 
facilitate the northward expansion and strengthening of a mid-
level ridge into the Great Lakes, tightening the upper-level 
geopotential gradient and associated jet (including upper-level 
diffluence in the region). The net result should be an increase 
in coverage of showers and storms along the stalled frontal 
boundary across northern Missouri, southern Iowa, central 
Illinois, and perhaps central Indiana overnight. It's difficult 
to say for sure where the primary axis of storms will be as 
often observed activity often verifies some 25 to 50 miles 
further south than depicted in CAM-guidance. With that said, 
persistent low- to upper-level forcing within the 2.0"+ PWAT 
regime will support torrential downpours and a threat for flash 
flooding tonight (especially near the IA/MO border where low-
level convergence will be maximized). Will broad-brush mid-range
likely (55-75%) PoPs generally along and south of I-80 for the 
overnight period. 

Coverage of showers and storms should begin to wane after 
daybreak as the low-level jet weakens and mid-level heights rise
(indicative of subsidence) along the northern flank of the 
strengthening mid- level ridge. With that said, do see a signal 
in CAM guidance for some sort of MCV or convectively augmented 
wave to propagate eastward along the stalled frontal zone during
the late morning and early afternoon hours south of I-80. 
Should that occur, showers and storms may continue unabated 
through the afternoon hours (again, mainly near and south of 
I-80). Confidence in the temperature forecast is hence pretty 
low tomorrow. Will simply stick with the inherited forecast 
calling for low 70s (north) to low 80s (south). 

Conceptually, do think there may be another round of storms in 
the general region tomorrow night through Thursday morning near 
the terminus of yet another low-level jet and beneath the right 
entrance region of the semi-perminent upper-level jet centered 
over the Upper Great Lakes. Based on the forecasted location of 
the terminus of the low-level jet across central Iowa, the main 
focus for storms may end up extending from eastern Iowa 
overnight and across northern Illinois by daybreak Thursday. 
Will broad-brush mid-range chance (45-55%) chance PoPs across 
the area in favor of refinement in later forecast packages. Like
tonight, there will be a threat for flash flooding tomorrow 
night given the continued high PWAT environment.
